_meta.indication: Topical treatment of external genital and perianal warts (Condylomata acuminata) in immunocompetent patients 18 years and older.

pivotal_trials.design: Randomized, double-blind, multi-center, three-arm, placebo-controlled, international trial (46 centers); patients randomized 2:2:1 to 15% ointment, 10% ointment, and vehicle, with treatment up to 16 weeks.
pivotal_trials.population: Adults at least 18 years of age with between 2 and 30 genital warts over a wart area between 2 and 600 mm2.
pivotal_trials.endpoint: Complete clearance of all baseline and new genital and perianal warts by week 16 of treatment.
pivotal_trials.result: Complete clearance: 15% ointment 50.7% (102/201) and 10% ointment 49.7% (99/199) vs vehicle 36.9% (38/103); p=0.0284 (15%) and p=0.0384 (10%) by Fisher's exact test.

pivotal_trials.design: Randomized, double-blind, multi-center, three-arm, placebo-controlled, international trial (50 centers, including the United States). The only difference from CT1017 was a protocol amendment adding a screening visit of up to 14 days; otherwise the design was identical, with patients randomized 2:2:1 to 15% ointment, 10% ointment, and vehicle and treatment up to 16 weeks.
pivotal_trials.population: Adult patients with external genital and perianal warts; 502 subjects included in the ITT population.
pivotal_trials.endpoint: Complete clearance of all baseline and new genital and perianal warts by week 16 of treatment.
pivotal_trials.result: Complete clearance: 15% ointment 56.6% (111/196) and 10% ointment 55.0% (111/202) vs vehicle 33.7% (35/104); p<0.001 for both doses by Fisher's exact test.

key_safety: Most common adverse reactions are local/application-site skin reactions: erythema (70% vs 32% vehicle), pruritus (69% vs 45%), burning (67% vs 31%), pain/discomfort (56% vs 14%), and erosion/ulceration (49% vs 10%). Local adverse events led to discontinuation or dose interruption in 5% (19/397); serious local adverse events of pain and inflammation occurred in two subjects (0.5%).
target_moa: The mode of action in clearing warts is unknown; the proposed mechanism of action is immunomodulatory. In vitro, kunecatechins (a mixture of catechins from green tea) had anti-oxidative activity of unknown clinical significance.
modality: Botanical drug product (topical ointment) — an extract of dried green tea leaves (kunecatechins, a mixture of catechins).

summary.text: Veregen was approved October 31, 2006 under a standard review NDA submitted under section 505(b)(1); it was the first botanical drug product approved in the United States since issuance of the Botanical Guidance. Approval was based on two pivotal phase 3 placebo-controlled trials (CT 1017 and CT 1018), with a postmarketing commitment for a phase 4 catechin pharmacokinetics study.

citations.quote: Please refer to your new drug application (NDA) dated September 23, 2005, received September 30, 2005, submitted under section 505(b)(1) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act for Veregen™ (kunecatechins) Ointment, 15%.
This is the first botanical drug product approved in the United States since issuance of the Botanical Guidance.
The two pivotal phase 3 trials were studies CT 1017 and CT 1018.

requirement.text: A phase 4 study comparing the pharmacokinetics of catechin following topical application of Veregen Ointment, 15%, with that obtained after oral administration of a green tea solution (two-arm study enrolling 20 evaluable patients and 20 evaluable healthy volunteers).
